newsitem.title: USA: Corporate culture blamed for Titanic disaster.
newsitem.headline: Corporate culture blamed for Titanic disaster.

text.p: The sinking of the Titanic was a management failure that put confidence ahead of safety, a senior U.S. official said on Thursday, blaming "corporate culture" for causing fatal plane, train and ship accidents.

National Transportation Safety Board chairman James Hall told a conference on corporate safety culture that the Titanic disaster was "one of the most famous examples of the negative influences corporate culture can exact on safety."

While mechanical and human failure were frequently cited as causes of accidents, corporate culture was often the underlying cause, he told a two-day meeting of 550 international business leaders, safety experts and government officials. The board is an independent U.S. government agency that investigates transport accidents.

Hall said the Titanic sailed on its maiden voyage from the British port of Southampton to New York 85 years ago unprepared for an accident. He said there were no binoculars for the crow's nest watch, the captain did not slow down or change course when warned of icefields in his path, the ship had lifeboats for barely half its passengers, and when the ship hit an iceberg many of the boats put to sea half-empty.
"The loss of the Titanic demonstrated the folly of management overconfidence in operation, leading to its failure to prepare for predictable, if unwelcome events," Hall said.

Asking why management accepted as true the boast that the Titanic was "unsinkable," he said the regulatory culture allowed these things to happen. "But where was the conscience, or just the common sense, of company management?"

He said investigators found that the captain refused to reduce his speed, "but if the investigators had stopped there we surely would have seen a repeat of the catastrophe," and there would not now be patrol boats in the Atlantic or lifeboats required for a ship's entire complement.
"The Titanic was a good example that the proximate cause is not the same as the probable cause; we must dig deeper to get to the true safety issue," he said.
Hall said "we understand that the best management in the world cannot overcome the influence of a corporate culture that is bent on emphasising other attributes over safety."

An example, he said, was the train driver who violates company rules by stopping between stations because he sees a potential safety threat, but by stopping to avoid the danger he has no way to prove an unsafe condition existed. "Is the train operator disciplined reflexively for his override of the rules or is he recognised for his alertness?" Hall asked.

He also blamed other accidents on corporate culture including a plane that crashed in poor weather because the pilot felt company pressure to fly and a train that derailed because management delayed maintenance to save money.
Hall added that there was a payoff for a good corporate safety culture because accidents could harm an entire industry through loss of sales and increasing government regulation.
"I think everyone here knows that it only takes one or two bad accidents unfortunately to sully the reputation of an entire industry," he said.
